function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
It contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Docker image for the Node.js app. |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Kubernetes Deployment (2 replicas). |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Kubernetes Service (ClusterIP). |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image, pushes it to your registry, and applies the manifests. |

> **NOTE** – The Dockerfile and Kubernetes manifests are written for a typical Express app that listens on port **3000**.  
> If your app uses a different port, change the `EXPOSE` line in the Dockerfile and the `containerPort`/`targetPort` values in the manifests.

---

## 1. Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Add the files

### 2.1 Dockerfile (root)

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Node 18 (Alpine) – small & secure
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the package files first – this allows Docker cache to be reused
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Tip** – If you have a `package-lock.json` or `yarn.lock`, copy that too.

### 2.2 Kubernetes manifests (`k8s/`)

Create a folder named `k8s` in the repo root and add the two files.

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Replace** `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo "${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}" | docker login -u "${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}" --password-stdin
        docker push <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
          k8s/service.yaml
        images: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the GitHub repo settings**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your registry username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your registry password / token  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig file (or use a dedicated action that pulls from a cluster)

> **If you’re using GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)**, you can skip the `docker login` step and use the `docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} -p ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` command instead.

---

## 3. Commit & push

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will run automatically.  
If everything is configured correctly, you’ll see:

1. The Docker image built and pushed to your registry.  
2. The Kubernetes manifests applied to your cluster (you can verify with `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get svc`, etc.).

---

## 4. Verify

```bash
# List pods
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome

# List services
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service

# Check logs of a pod
kubectl logs <pod-name>
```

If you’re using a LoadBalancer or NodePort, you can access the app via the external IP/port.

---

### Quick checklist

- [ ] Dockerfile uses `node:18-alpine` and exposes port 3000.  
- [ ] Kubernetes manifests reference the correct image registry.  
- [ ] GitHub Actions secrets are set (`DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, `KUBECONFIG`).  
- [ ] Workflow pushes the image tagged with the commit SHA.  
- [ ] Deployment uses 2 replicas (adjust if needed).  

That’s it! 🎉  
Feel free to tweak the number of replicas, add environment variables, or extend the CI pipeline as your project grows.
